input.question: How/Why did organisms go from single cell division to requiring a separate partner to reproduce?
input.ground_truth: I've always tied it to the invention of meiosis. Mitosis divides cells, but meiosis make half-cell kits, that can then combine in rapidly expanding numbers of ways. I see it as several billion years of mitosis and then meiosis gets discovered and boom: Cambrian Explosion.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How/Why did organisms go from single cell division to requiring a separate partner to reproduce?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a toy block. At first, you can just make more blocks by copying the one you have. You split it in half and each half grows into a new block. That’s like how the very first tiny living things (called single-celled organisms) made more of themselves—they just split in two.

But as time went on, some of these tiny living things started working together. It was like having two different kinds of blocks that fit together to make a bigger and better castle. When two different blocks (or living things) come together, their castle (or baby living thing) can be even stronger and better at surviving.

So, instead of just splitting in half by themselves, some living things started needing a friend to help make new babies. This helped them make stronger and healthier babies, and that’s why some living things started needing a partner to reproduce!
